thread.title: Never Drone Alone - Commentary Magazine

author: Arthur Herman
title: Never Drone Alone - Commentary Magazine
text:
The war in Ukraine has brought conceits once known only to science-fiction geeks into the real world, as rival armies of robots take over the skies and even the seas surrounding that embattled country. There are hunter-killer drones, kamikaze drones, mine-laying drones, mine-detecting drones, even “dragon drones” equipped with flamethrowers that bring a touch of Game of Thrones to the conversation. Uncrewed machines dominate virtually every strategic and tactical operation and scenario in the conflict. According to the Institute for the Study of War, uncrewed ground vehicles (UGVs) and airborne drones account for up to 90 percent of military activity in “hot” combat zones like Pokrovsk.
Thus has the battlefield morphed into a robotic ecosystem in which low-cost, off-the-shelf quadcopters and marine vessels without a person on them have become logistical workhorses and primary strike weapons.
To many military history experts, this represents a revolution in military affairs comparable to the arrival of mechanized blitzkrieg warfare in World War II—or even the advent of gunpowder. The key to victory is mass production at scale, i.e., producing quantities with no loss in quality. Each month, 200,000 drones are delivered to Ukrainian troops—up tenfold from 2024. Ukraine is aiming to produce more than 4 million drones annually—an industrial mobilization effort that signals just how important these unmanned systems have become.
The Russians have also proven to be good at uncrewed warfare—even deploying turbojet drones in their latest round of attacks on Kyiv, and drones using AI to guide to targets. But the true masters of this new form of warfare are the Ukrainians, in part because it’s the only way they can confront an enemy with more soldiers, more weapons, and more resources—and survive.
The United States doesn’t face that same existential threat—or at least not yet—as it struggles to seize the future lead in this drone revolution away from rivals like China and Russia. But fortunately, it has its own example of victory by mass production at scale, during World War II.
As the Hudson Institute’s Can Kasapoğlu has written, “Ukraine’s wartime technological transformation has been driven by the state and a dense ecosystem of private technology firms, start-ups, volunteer engineers, and Western commercial partners.”
This was almost exactly what American industry achieved in the crucial 18 months before entering World War II and before perfecting the system during the war itself—relying at the time on commercial partners here at home instead of a multinational collaborative alliance like the one Ukraine is relying on today.
Between the two—our own experience in World War II and Ukraine’s experience today—we can draw certain key lessons both for military and for industry.
_____________
We can start by taking a closer look at what’s happening in the unfriendly skies over Ukraine.
Both Ukraine and Russia have learned that uncrewed systems—drones—have a much larger, even indispensable role to play on the modern battlefield than the limited role they played in America’s recent conflicts, as either intelligence and reconnaissance platforms or for whack-a-mole precision strikes in remote places like Afghanistan.
The founders of drone warfare are the Israelis. They have been designing and exporting military drones for more than five decades, going back to the IAI Scout they used during the 1982 war in Lebanon. Israeli companies still produce top-quality medium- to high-altitude long-endurance (MALE) platforms like the Hermes 900 and Heron series. The IDF has also been carefully integrating artificial intelligence capabilities into its command-and-control software, like “Server in the Sky” and “Storm Clouds” drone arrays. Additionally, they use advanced computer vision to map, classify, and generate real-time target data across battlefields like those in Gaza.
The war in Ukraine, however, has placed a premium on sheer numbers over exquisite tech for dominating the uncrewed battle space. The Ukrainians discovered they needed mass-produced, low-cost but versatile weapons that can spot and target the enemy with precision while providing constant feedback to their operators. These are now the key—not only to reducing the number of human casualties, especially on the Ukrainian side, but also to disrupting the conventional war plans of the enemy.
At first, the war started with both sides relying on classic MALE drones, first to identify targets such as enemy tanks and vehicles, then to take them out with missile strikes. When Russian air defenses caught on to the Ukrainian method and made MALE operations too costly for Kyiv, the Ukrainians shifted to one-way attack (OWA) systems like the Liutyi, the Ukrainian version of the Iranian Shahed, which Russia and Iran manufacture at a joint plant in Yelabuga, Tatarstan. These kamikaze-style attackers aim at infrastructure targets such as Russian airfields, military-industrial plants, and oil-production facilities.
The heyday of the OWA systems was just a year ago. Today, the growth industry is in even smaller and deadlier drones, each weighing around 300 pounds with a nine-mile range. They are known as First Person View (FPV) systems because pilots in control rooms far from the battleground wear specialized video goggles to see a live video feed from the drone’s onboard camera. Costing in some cases as little as $500 to make, these copter drones zoom in very close to the actual battlefield, for either reconnaissance or lethal kills. That makes it hard for troops or frontline equipment to hide or evade detection. FPVs operate effectively in massed close-range precision assaults, while midrange versions fly 30 to 100 kilometers or more behind the front lines, in order to target supply convoys, fuel depots, and command centers.
These and myriad other variants of uncrewed warfare—the low-flying dragon drones armed with incendiary munitions, not to mention undersea drones that Ukraine has used to cripple Russian naval power in the Black Sea—have become ubiquitous on all fronts and for all operations. Today the Ukrainians deploy approximately 9,000 drones per day for a variety of combat, intelligence, and logistical tasks.
Some experts question whether this shift to unmanned systems really spells the end of conventional manned warfare or is just another stage in its ongoing evolution. Others wonder (with reason) whether drones will really provide a decisive edge if the U.S. and China ever come to blows, compared with the impact of anti-satellite warfare in space or electronic and cyber warfare, let alone nuclear weapons. Nonetheless, no one doubts that winning the unmanned skies of the future is going to be a priority for our military—and our defense industry.
With its recently announced Drone Dominance Program, the Pentagon plans to produce 200,000 by 2027. To hit that number, it’s going to need to make some major changes in how it buys what it needs, and from whom.
Fortunately, what Ukraine has had to learn out of necessity, we can learn by looking back to the last time we fought a war that depended on mass production of airpower at scale. Nine decades ago.
In 1940, the United States had virtually no effective air force at all compared with Germany or Britain or even France. When President Roosevelt called for a program to build 50,000 military and naval planes a year to defend America, aviation experts pronounced the figure “hysterical chatter.”
Yet just two years later, aircraft production in the United States almost reached that number. In 1943, production zoomed past it, at more than 84,000. By war’s end, the United States had built more than 350,000 planes. In 1944, its factories and facilities were producing a warplane every five minutes. How we made crewed military aircraft was very similar to what Ukraine is doing with uncrewed systems.
We can look at three ways in which U.S. industry can emulate the Ukrainian example by invoking the defense production lessons of the past, in order to make sure we ourselves never lose our uncrewed edge—and all without having to go to war.
The first: Cast your production net wide.
When President Franklin Roosevelt asked General Motors President William Knudsen in the summer of 1940 to help him get the country ready for modern war, Knudsen knew immediately they could never achieve the numbers of aircraft needed by sticking to the traditional aerospace companies: Martin, Lockheed, Douglas, Grumman, and the others. In 1938, for example, those firms had barely supplied the Army Air Corps with 90 planes a month.
Instead, Knudsen turned the problem over to his colleagues in the automobile industry, knowing they had the biggest industrial facilities in the country but also the biggest engineering staffs whose job it was to solve problems.
He started by asking them to produce aircraft engines and aircraft parts. Eventually the more intrepid automakers volunteered to make entire airplanes using the aircraft companies’ designs. Ford’s partnership with North American, designer of the B-24 bomber, wound up producing more than 15,000 planes; GM’s partnership with Roy Grumman’s company saw thousands of Avenger torpedo bombers and Wildcat fighters come off the assembly line.
In the end, GM would end up producing 10 percent of all wartime materiel in the U.S., including airplanes, airplane engines, and a staggering array of components for America’s leading aircraft manufacturers—all things GM had never made before the war started. The lesson is, turning to the most productive companies, large and small, can serve to break the bottleneck.
Before the war in Ukraine started, the country had just seven companies that produced drones. Today Ukraine has approximately 450 to 500 companies in that line of work. Hundreds of small firms and workshops drive the massive private output of FPV and strike drones, while about 40 to 50 companies are considered the top-tier market leaders. Meanwhile there are dozens of highly specialized firms focused entirely on sub-components such as batteries and optical systems, as well as interceptor drones like Wild Hornets. All this sprang up spontaneously from the impact of the Russian invasion.
William Knudsen and FDR had the advantage of a massive industrial economy at their beck and call, but it still needed to be converted and retooled, company by company, assembly line by assembly line, to make things almost all of them had never made before, from tanks, artillery pieces, and aircraft engines to combat helmets, ammunition boxes, and optical equipment for airborne gun cameras.
Today’s American defense industry is far more able and innovative, and it makes a bewildering variety of military equipment for war in the skies, on the ground, and at sea—even in space. But in the last several decades, its focus has been on building exquisite high-precision systems instead of throwaway versions (not to mention dealing with the cost in time and money required to navigate the traditional Pentagon procurement process).
We were much closer to the Ukraine model during World War II, or even before, when Knudsen and his colleagues began to mobilize commercial industry. As Knudsen told his colleagues, “If we get into war, the winning of it will be purely a matter of material and production,” whether it was planes, tanks, machine guns, submarines, or torpedoes—all categories in which the Axis Powers at first enjoyed a firm technological advantage.
Likewise, the challenges that today’s defense industry would face involve a shift to producing quantity over quality. We need to be able to mass-produce battle-ready hardware at a consumer-electronics pace while also decoupling supply chains from foreign dependencies. That can be mitigated by expanding the number of manufacturing firms that get contracts to build the drones needed for future warfare.
That points to the second lesson: Innovation follows productivity, not the other way around.
In 1940–1941, the Japanese Zero, the German Messerschmitt Bf 109, and even the Italian Macchi C.202 Folgore set the standard for fighter design and effectiveness, both operationally and in numbers. Knudsen knew that in the first two years of converting to war production, the United States would be locked into building planes of inferior quality, like the Curtiss P-40. But he also believed that, as time went on, American companies would discover how to bake innovation into future versions and that such innovation would spawn a dozen new, more effective designs.
As a result, the flying machines American companies were building in 1940–1941 were very different from the ones they were building by 1943–1944. Early versions of the B-17 Flying Fortress gave way to improved versions, then to the B-29 Superfortress. Even the P-51 Mustang, America’s premier fighter plane of the war, was a far more powerful and versatile airplane in 1944 than the version that first flew in 1941.
Ukraine’s drone industry has followed a very similar trajectory. The drones initially used when Ukraine faced virtual national extinction in 2022 are very different from the sophisticated systems that top-tier manufacturers like Ukrspecsystems, Skyeton, Athlon Avia, UkrJet, and Terminal Autonomy are now making, with the development of tactical-operational drones, loitering munitions, and interceptors.
Likewise, production innovations like modular design, frontline reassembly, and tight feedback loops have allowed Ukraine to build and improve much faster than traditional defense systems.
The same will be true with the biggest innovation of all: artificial intelligence. It is the key to making drone technology decisive, from coordinating massive swarms of drones in attack or defense to helping systems operate in electronically jammed environments and track targets without continuous human control. We’re not there yet. As the Pentagon’s 2023 Replicator drone program demonstrated, attempts to integrate AI from the start haven’t worked out as hoped. The temptation to put the innovation cart before the production horse can be irresistible for administrators. Letting the production process discover where innovation is truly needed is more effective.
This leads directly to the third lesson: Stick close to the warfighter.
Typically, the production line in a Ukraine drone factory looks like any other UAV assembly line. First, carbon-fiber frames come off the line; then workers attach the motors, props, and other components; then the final product is shipped.
What’s different is the Ukrainian “reverse cycle” approach to production. Many manufacturers send completed systems to the front line, where units have their own assembly facilities. They actually disassemble the drones and reassemble them according to their specific battlefield needs.
This happened constantly during World War II as well. “Field modification” became a byword for aircraft manufacturers as the machines they rolled off the assembly line were transformed in the hands of the mechanics and aircrews who actually had to use them in combat.
In the Southwest Pacific, the Fifth Air Force’s maverick mechanic Irving “Pappy” Gunn and manufacturer’s field representative Jack Fox tore out the bombardier’s compartment from North American’s B-25 and mounted heavy machine guns (even a 75 mm cannon!) in the plane’s nose in order to turn the B-25 from a regular medium bomber into a deadly commerce raider to use against Japanese shipping.
General Curtis LeMay did something similar with the B-29 Superfortress. He took out all the expensive gun turrets except the one in the rear, as well as seats for the co-pilot and bombardier, to use the plane for devastating low-level attacks on Japan’s urban and industrial centers.
Back home, Grumman Aircraft CEO Roy Grumman kept his office door open in order to hear from Navy pilots flying his F4F Wildcat what changes needed to be made to compete with Japan’s high-flying and highly maneuverable Japanese Zero—changes that led to the creation of the Grumman F6F Hellcat, which came to dominate the skies in the Pacific theater.
As I noted in a 2011 COMMENTARY article titled “How Israel’s Defense Industry Can Help Save America,” the Israel Defense Forces do something similar with virtually all the equipment they receive from the U.S., tearing out some features and adding others, in order to fit with Israel’s own battlefield needs.
American defense companies can do the same by forming early R&D relationships with the frontline forces that will be using their products. Together with regular communication and the ability to adapt—i.e., not being stuck on turning out one particular final product—defense companies and the Pentagon can also make sure that a drone end product can be quickly assembled and disassembled. This will allow the warfighter to, in effect, “plug and play” by adding whatever payload, sensor, camera, or video transmitter he might need.
Sticking close to the warfighter and decentralizing innovation will be a lot easier than it was during World War II, thanks to 3D printing systems for manufacturing drones, parts, and munitions directly at the edge of operations, instead of waiting for shipments from the home factory. So will adoption of AI as a tool for high-speed, flexible manufacturing processes and as a weapon for next-generation drone warfare.
Turning to smaller, more agile companies that can move in with quick solutions to battlefield challenges will also facilitate this change. Too many of today’s small defense start-ups run into trouble trying to shift from their first R&D contracts to full-scale government procurement, expiring in an innovation-killing “valley of death” inside the Pentagon. A new streamlined model for drone procurement and manufacturing can push defense acquisition timelines closer to those of commercial, consumer-based production velocities while freeing up small, innovative firms so they can do what they do best.
“Small is beautiful” won’t just be true for drones themselves, as we’ve learned in Ukraine. It may be the future motto for drone makers as well. A few thousand square feet in an office park outside Austin, Texas, or Green Bay, Wisconsin, with a “pop-up” shop located outside an Air Force or Navy base armed with a 3D printer, AI software, and a garage with bays for quick assembly and disassembly—such modest facilities could become the seedbeds of a military revolution, or at least a future Lockheed or Grumman or Anduril.
The enemy always gets a vote, so, of course, countermeasures by a real or prospective foe—e.g., electromagnetic jamming and reducing and/or “spoofing” hardware signatures to fool the machines—will inevitably reduce the impact of a revolution like this.
But as always in warfare, countermeasures then spawn counter-countermeasures, which are the heart of a true revolution in military affairs. That’s because an RMA does not depend on the weapons themselves, whether cannons and muskets or armored tanks and drones. It rests on new doctrines, organizations, and military and industrial strategies that integrate those weapons into operational plans, and then into strategic dominance.
The world is moving closer to a similar breakthrough with uncrewed systems. America’s warfighters and their industrial partners have an opportunity to lead the way forward by learning from their own past and partnering with the masters of drone warfare today to build for the future.
